1:
Hi everyone. This talk is about a device whose active part is a single atom: one phosphorus or arsenic atom in silicon, put there with a scanning tunneling microscope. Physically, that atom acts like a hydrogen atom living inside a semiconductor. One extra electron, held by a weakened Coulomb pull. And in EE one forty-three terms, every step is a process you already know: resist, lithography, gas-phase doping, an anneal, epitaxy, etch and metal. The difference is that the resist is one atom thick, and the dose is one molecule.

If asked: Is the image real data? No, it's a render. Every microscope image later in the talk is real measured data.
2: Three ideas run through the whole talk. One: precision. One lattice site on the silicon surface is zero point three eight nanometers, and that's the placement error we can reach. Two: yield. If each site works with probability p, an array of n sites works with p to the n. So p has to be really close to one. Three: speed. A tip writes about a hundred atoms per second, and that sets the limit. Act one is why one atom makes a good qubit. Act two is how it's built. Act three is does it work. Act four is how it scales. Keep one question in mind: how do you put exactly one atom exactly where you want it?
3:
Think of the donor as hydrogen inside a dielectric. The Bohr radius scales with the dielectric constant, times the free mass over the effective mass. Silicon has a big dielectric constant and a small effective mass, so hydrogen's zero point zero five nanometers stretches to about two nanometers. You get two spins for free: the electron and the phosphorus nucleus. Two times two gives a four-level system. Electron spins are driven with ESR, nuclear spins with NMR. Readout turns spin into charge. A spin-up electron can tunnel into a nearby single-electron transistor, a spin-down one can't, and the transistor current changes. In purified silicon twenty-eight, only about two hundred parts per million of silicon twenty-nine is left, so stray nuclear spins are rare. That's why implanted donors there reach thirty-five point six seconds of coherence, and gates near ninety-nine point nine nine percent.

If asked: Is it really hydrogen-like? To first order, yes. Silicon's six conduction-band valleys split the ground state.
4:
Two-qubit gates use exchange, called J, which comes from the two electron wavefunctions overlapping. The wavefunction squared dies off exponentially: e to the minus two r over the Bohr radius. So the coupling drops exponentially as the donors move apart. Quick estimate: move one donor by one lattice site, and that term shrinks by e to the minus zero point three eight, about zero point seven. That's roughly a thirty percent change in coupling from a one-site mistake. On top of that, silicon's valleys make J jump around from site to site. So precision isn't optional. The map is drawn to scale: two donors thirteen nanometers apart.

If asked: Can't you just tune J with gates? Yes, but only within a window set by where the atoms are.
5:
Ion implantation is random. It's a Poisson process. If the average number of ions per site is lambda, the chance of exactly one is lambda times e to the minus lambda. That peaks at lambda equals one, where the chance is one over e, about thirty-seven percent. So without counting ions, no dose ever beats thirty-seven percent. Those bars are that distribution. Even with the best ion counting, up to ninety-nine point eight five percent confidence at fourteen kilo-electron-volts, each ion still stops at a random spot, spread over nanometers. STM placement is locked to the lattice, plus or minus one site, and arsenic windows give ninety-seven percent single atoms.

If asked: What about lower energy? The spread shrinks, but it never gets down to one lattice site.
6:
Here's the device as an EE spec sheet. Substrate: silicon, purified silicon twenty-eight for qubits. Dopants: phosphorus from phosphine, or arsenic from arsine. Placement: plus or minus zero point three eight nanometers. Leads: doped sheets around ten to the fourteen per square centimeter, under one nanometer thick. That's a two-D electron gas. The Kane design on the right needs about one tesla and about a tenth of a kelvin. That way the spin's Zeeman energy is way bigger than the thermal energy, and the spin starts polarized. A-gates tune the hyperfine. J-gates tune the exchange between donors about ten nanometers apart.

If asked: Why millikelvin? Thermal energy has to sit far below the Zeeman splitting, so the spin starts in a known state.
7:
Read the timeline as a list of solved physics problems. Nineteen ninety-four: a tip strips hydrogen off silicon by exciting the silicon-hydrogen bond. That's a lithography. Nineteen ninety-eight: the proposal that donor nuclear spins can be qubits. Two thousand three: single phosphorus atoms placed on purpose. Twenty twelve: a transistor whose channel is one atom. Twenty nineteen: a fast exchange gate and three-D stacking. Twenty twenty to twenty twenty-four: arsenic chemistry pushes single-atom yield to ninety-seven percent, and light starts replacing the tip for coarse patterning. Twenty twenty-five: four- and eleven-qubit processors. Same recipe every time: passivate, pattern, dose, anneal, cap.

If asked: Why did it take so long? Each step needed a new way to measure what was happening.
8:
Neil Curson's group at UCL works on the materials physics underneath this platform. Three threads. One, dopant chemistry: swapping phosphine for arsine, which breaks apart about a thousand times faster. In Arrhenius terms, that's like lowering the barrier by k T times the log of a thousand, about zero point one eight electron-volts at room temperature. Two, metrology: imaging buried layers with X-ray fluorescence without destroying them, and using photoemission to see electrons squeezed into less than a nanometer. Three, scaling: showing that extreme ultraviolet light can strip the same hydrogen resist. Plus arsenic in germanium, which goes in at room temperature.

If asked: Why arsenic? It breaks apart faster, so it needs fewer free sites, so the windows can be smaller.
9:
This is the process traveler, with the EE one forty-three module for each step. The key rule is thermal history: hot steps first, then everything at five hundred degrees C or below. Steps one to three clean and passivate the surface. Step four is lithography. Steps five and six are gas doping and activation, at three hundred fifty degrees. Steps seven and eight bury the dopants with epitaxy at two hundred fifty. Steps nine to eleven are alignment, etch, aluminum contacts, and testing. The design rule is diffusion. Diffusion length is two root D t, and D goes up exponentially with temperature. So the hottest step after patterning sets the whole budget.

If asked: Which step limits throughput? Step four, the tip.
10:
Surface prep. Outgas for over eight hours at six hundred degrees, then flash to about twelve hundred. That burns off the oxide and carbon, and leaves clean rows of silicon dimers. The STM chamber sits below five times ten to the minus eleven millibar. Why so low? At ten to the minus six torr, a surface picks up about one monolayer per second. At ten to the minus eleven, one monolayer takes on the order of a day. Then atomic hydrogen at three hundred thirty degrees for five minutes caps every dangling bond. That single layer is the resist. Inert where it's there, reactive where it's been removed.

If asked: Why three thirty? Hot enough to get a clean monohydride layer, but below where the hydrogen leaves.
11:
STM lithography is controlled tunneling. The current goes as e to the minus two kappa d, and kappa is about one per angstrom. So every angstrom of tip height changes the current by about e squared. That's seven to eight times. That's why the tip can see single atoms. To write, you raise the bias, and the electrons break silicon-hydrogen bonds. Check the line dose: it's current divided by speed. Ten nanoamps over ten nanometers per second is one coulomb per meter. That's the quoted ten to the minus two coulombs per centimeter. Arsenic windows use three point five volts and three thousand picoamps, at fifty nanometers per second. Two dimers each, four point six nanometers apart.

If asked: Is this like e-beam lithography? Yes. Dose is charge per length, and the resist is one atom thick.
12:
Dosing is gas kinetics. The flux of molecules hitting the surface is the pressure, over root two pi m k T. For arsine at five times ten to the minus nine millibar and room temperature, that's about nine times ten to the eleven molecules per square centimeter per second. Over ten minutes, that's about zero point eight arrivals per surface site. So each window sees about one molecule, and the hydrogen resist rejects the rest. Phosphine loses its hydrogens step by step, over minutes. Arsine breaks apart about a thousand times faster, in tens of seconds. Arsenic coverage maxes out at about a quarter of the sites.

If asked: Why not a full layer? Coverage stops at a quarter no matter the dose rate. So surface chemistry sets the limit, not the gas supply.
13:
Incorporation needs heat, but not too much. At three hundred fifty degrees, k T is about fifty-four milli-electron-volts. That's enough for the arsenic or phosphorus to swap into the top silicon layer. But it's below three hundred eighty, where hydrogen starts leaving and the resist fails. So a thirty-degree window separates working from failing. Each arsenic that goes in kicks out exactly one silicon atom onto the surface. Arsenic in, silicon out. So counting the kicked-out silicon counts your dopants, right there in the chamber. In EE one forty-three terms, this is the drive-in anneal, with basically zero diffusion length.

If asked: What limits the window? The energy barrier for hydrogen leaving the silicon.
14:
Burying the dopants is a thermal-budget trade-off. Good crystal wants heat. Keeping the atoms in place wants cold. Phosphorus grown over at two hundred fifty degrees drifts about five nanometers up toward the surface. For arsenic: two nanometers grown unheated to lock the atoms down. Then a five hundred degree anneal for fifteen seconds. Then twenty-eight nanometers at two hundred fifty. At zero point zero zero three nanometers per second, those twenty-eight nanometers take about two point six hours. Textbook diffusion numbers say that anneal should barely move anything. But the measured layer is limited by arsenic diffusion. So at these huge concentrations, the real diffusivity must be higher than the textbook value. That's why the anneal is only fifteen seconds.

If asked: Why not grow it all cold? Cold silicon only grows as a crystal up to a critical thickness. Past that, it turns amorphous.
15:
Connecting to the buried device is normal microfab, just with extreme alignment. Etched markers plus a combined STM and SEM, or Kelvin-probe imaging of the buried pattern, line up the contacts with ninety-five percent yield over more than a hundred fifty devices. You can't see the layer optically. It's a sheet of electrons thirty nanometers down. Hall bars are twenty by two hundred microns, made with optical lithography and reactive ion etching. Aluminum goes into holes etched through the doped layer. Transport is measured at one point eight kelvin, and the qubits run at millikelvin.

If asked: Why is the aluminum contact ohmic? The layer is so heavily doped that the barrier is thin enough to tunnel straight through.
16:
Electrical proof uses sheet resistance. For a two-D sheet, R s equals one over q times N s times mu. Measured: sixteen hundred ohms per square, and a mobility of twenty-eight square centimeters per volt second. Solve for N s, and you get about one point four times ten to the fourteen per square centimeter. The surface has about six point eight times ten to the fourteen atoms per square centimeter. So that's about one dopant for every five surface sites. Activation is eighty-one percent, or eighty-eight percent after a five hundred sixty degree anneal. Photoemission shows the electrons squeezed into less than a nanometer, and arsenic confines better than phosphorus.

If asked: Why is the mobility so low? The electrons scatter off the ionized dopants they came from, all packed into one atomic plane.
17:
Two proofs that this works. On the left: single phosphorus atoms in windows about one nanometer across, three dimers, written at four volts and one nanoamp. Then dosed, annealed at three hundred fifty, and landing about twelve nanometers apart. On the right: a transistor whose island is one phosphorus atom. Its transport shows Coulomb blockade. The charging energy of a single atom is huge, so current only flows when a discrete atomic level lines up with the leads. That gives sharp conductance peaks as you sweep the gate voltage.

If asked: Why does it work at four kelvin? The single-atom charging energy is far above the thermal energy there.
18:
Yield is a product of probabilities. If each site works independently with probability p, an n-site array works with p to the n. Phosphorus in an ideal window works sixty-three percent of the time, and under seventy percent in bigger windows. Zero point seven to the sixteen is about a third of a percent. For fifty donors at sixty-three percent, it's about one in ten billion. Flip it around: the biggest array you can make half the time is about two sites for phosphorus, and about twenty-three for arsenic at ninety-seven percent. The band shows how sensitive this is. Arsenic at ninety-five to ninety-nine percent gives forty-four to eighty-five percent for sixteen sites.

If asked: Are the failures really independent? The formula assumes so. Correlated failures would change the math.
19:
Arsenic's fix is a geometry rule. Arsine breaks apart fast, so one molecule needs fewer free sites. A four-site window, two dimers, takes exactly one. Single-atom yield is ninety-seven percent, plus or minus two, with each atom placed within four lattice sites. At ninety-seven percent, a two-by-two array would come out perfect about eighty-nine percent of the time. The first perfect two-by-two was actually made with windows of two to eight sites. The ninety-seven percent comes from the later four-site statistics. And you can retry the failed sites. A second try multiplies the failure chance, which pushes p toward one.

If asked: Why not three sites? Smaller windows let hydrogen grab the site back before the arsine lands.
20:
The same chemistry carries over. On germanium, arsine goes in at room temperature with no anneal, and the hydrogen leaves by three hundred thirty degrees. If a reaction happens on its own at room temperature, its barrier has to be under about zero point eight electron-volts. That comes from an attempt rate of about ten to the thirteen per second: the rate only stays above once per second up to about thirty k T. Bismuth goes the other way. It's a heavy donor, delivered by a molecule called triphenyl-bismuth, about a nanometer across. Its side groups come off near one hundred forty degrees, and bismuth goes in near three hundred sixty. That's close to the three hundred eighty degree limit of the hydrogen resist.

If asked: Why germanium? Donors there have bigger Bohr radii and a stronger Stark effect. But this talk stays with silicon.
21:
Now the qubits. Twenty nineteen: an exchange gate between two donor electrons in about eight hundred picoseconds. Plus a three-D device with layers aligned better than five nanometers, and ninety-seven point nine percent readout. Twenty twenty-five: a four-qubit processor. Three phosphorus nuclei sharing one electron, at one point four five tesla and fifteen millikelvin, with two-qubit gate fidelities of ninety-nine point three to ninety-nine point six five percent. And an eleven-qubit processor: two registers thirteen nanometers apart. The best Bell fidelities are ninety-nine point five percent inside a register, and ninety-seven percent across. Be careful comparing: twenty nineteen used natural silicon and electron spins, twenty twenty-five used silicon twenty-eight and nuclear spins.

If asked: Why nuclear spins? They hold their coherence much longer.
22:
Here's the physics in one equation. Three terms: electron Zeeman, nuclear Zeeman, and hyperfine. Three nuclei, with hyperfine values of six, sixty-eight, and one hundred three megahertz. Each one shifts the electron's frequency up or down by half its value. Two to the three gives eight ESR lines. Check: the full spread is six plus sixty-eight plus one hundred three. That's one hundred seventy-seven megahertz, exactly the gap between the outer lines. So the electron's frequency reads out the nuclear register. Thermal check: the electron sits near two hundred millikelvin. h f at thirty-nine gigahertz is about nine times k T, so the electron is still almost fully polarized. Coherence: about twenty-eight microseconds for the electron, and half a millisecond to one point three milliseconds for the nuclei.

If asked: Why does the hyperfine change with electric field? Gate voltages reshape the electron wavefunction at the nucleus.
23:
Entanglement is checked with state tomography. You measure in lots of bases and rebuild the density matrix. For a perfect Bell state, the matrix has four equal corners of one half, and nothing else. Fidelity is the overlap with that ideal. All three nuclear pairs hit ninety-six point eight to ninety-seven point seven percent. The GHZ state ties all three nuclei together, at ninety-six point two percent. Then Grover's search on three qubits. With eight possible answers, the ideal success after two rounds is ninety-four point five percent. The hardware got ninety-three point five. That's ninety-eight point nine percent of ideal.

If asked: Why two rounds? A third round overshoots the answer and lowers the probability.
24:
Dopant arrays can also simulate many-body physics. The Hubbard model has two energies: hopping, called t, set by tunneling between dots, and on-site repulsion, called U. Hopping drops exponentially with spacing. So stretching a three-by-three lattice from four point one to ten point seven nanometers takes U over t from small, which is a metal, to large, which is a Mott insulator, where repulsion freezes the electrons in place. A ten-dot chain with alternating couplings builds the SSH model. When the hopping inside each cell is weaker than the hopping between cells, the chain is topological, with edge states at zero energy. You see two conductance peaks instead of ten.

If asked: Why use dopants for this? Lithographic precision sets the hopping directly.
25:
Throughput is an EE scaling problem. In precise mode, a tip writes about a hundred atoms per second. One square centimeter of silicon has about seven times ten to the fourteen surface sites. Writing that one atom at a time takes about two hundred fifteen thousand years. At two volts and hundreds of nanoamps, the tip goes a thousand nanometers per second and still keeps its resolution. Precision is only lost in field-emission mode. EUV lithography exposes the equivalent of ten to the fourteen nanometers per second. That's eleven to thirteen orders of magnitude faster, because every photon exposes in parallel. Even ten million tips across a wafer would still be way too slow.

If asked: Can tips just go faster? Speed trades directly against precision.
26:
EUV can strip the same hydrogen resist. Photon energy is h c over lambda. Industrial thirteen and a half nanometer light is about ninety-two electron-volts, and clear hydrogen removal showed up at ninety-three and one hundred six. It works indirectly. The silicon absorbs the photons and spits out secondary electrons, and those electrons break the silicon-hydrogen bonds. Same physics as under the tip. The cost is dose: up to eighteen thousand joules per square centimeter, which means exposures on the order of minutes with three hundred watt sources. The plan: EUV for the leads and wiring, STM for the qubit cores.

If asked: What's the resolution? Diffraction limits EUV to roughly ten nanometers.
27:
Our prototype applies these design rules with real numbers. Four arsenic atoms, one per four-site window, four point six nanometers apart. A single-electron transistor seventeen nanometers away for readout, and two gates. All of it made of doped arsenic in one plane, buried thirty nanometers deep. Expected yield: zero point nine seven to the fourth, about eighty-nine percent. Scale up to sixteen sites, and it's sixty-one percent for arsenic versus zero point three percent for phosphorus. So how big a register you can build is set by chemistry, through p, not by lithography.

If asked: What sets the seventeen nanometer spacing? Sensor sensitivity versus tunnel coupling. It's an exponential trade-off.
28:
Here's the traveler as numbers. Hot steps first: a twelve hundred degree flash and a six hundred degree outgas. After patterning, the hottest step is a five hundred degree anneal for fifteen seconds. Then three hundred fifty for incorporation, and two hundred fifty for overgrowth. Why that order works: diffusion goes up exponentially with temperature. So that short five hundred degree step dominates everything after patterning, and it sets the final width. Compare our own lab: a ten fifty degree drive-in for about forty minutes moves phosphorus hundreds of nanometers. Same physics, opposite goal.

If asked: Where's the risk? The anneal. Too hot or too long, and the layer spreads out.
29:
Three takeaways. Precision: placement is set by the lattice, zero point three eight nanometers, and exchange depends exponentially on spacing, so precision is a must. Yield: arrays work with p to the n. Arsenic pushed p to ninety-seven percent, which moves the half-yield array size from about two sites to about twenty-three. Throughput: writing a hundred atoms per second can't cover a wafer, so parallel light on the same hydrogen resist is the bridge. And the quantum tests passed: an eight-line spectrum, Bell states near ninety-seven percent, and Grover at ninety-eight point nine percent of ideal. Thank you.

If asked: What comes next? Bigger registers, which is exactly the p to the n problem.
30: Not presented. Equation sheet for questions, written the way you'd say it. Bohr radius: dielectric constant, times free mass over effective mass, times the hydrogen Bohr radius. Chance of exactly one ion: lambda e to the minus lambda. Its max is one over e, at lambda equals one. Exchange: falls as e to the minus two R over the Bohr radius. Tunneling current: goes as e to the minus two kappa d, with kappa about one per angstrom. Line dose: current over speed. Gas flux: pressure over root two pi m k T. Sheet resistance: one over q N s mu. Hall density: current times field, over q times the Hall voltage. Diffusion length: two root D t, where D is D naught times e to the minus E a over k T. Array yield: p to the n. Half-yield array size: log of one half over log of p.
31: Not presented. Equation sheet, part two. Spin Hamiltonian: electron Zeeman, plus nuclear Zeeman for each nucleus, plus the hyperfine coupling for each nucleus. ESR lines sit at the center frequency, plus or minus half of each A. Polarization needs h f much bigger than k T: about one hundred sixty micro-electron-volts versus seventeen at two hundred millikelvin. That gives ninety-nine point nine eight percent. Off-resonance flip: at most omega squared over omega squared plus delta squared. Bell fidelity: the overlap of the ideal state with the measured density matrix. Grover success: sine squared of two r plus one, times theta, where sine theta is one over root N. Hubbard: minus t times hopping, plus U times double occupancy. Mott regime when U is much bigger than t. EUV photon energy: h c over lambda. Resolution: k one lambda over N A.
32: Backup. Alternate titles, plus the four-by-four arsenic array. With non-ideal windows, ten to twelve of the fifteen checked sites held single atoms. That's up to eighty percent. It's a good check on p to the n. At eighty percent, a perfect sixteen-site array happens zero point eight to the sixteen, about three percent of the time. That's why the perfect demo was a small two-by-two. Window shape matters as much as chemistry. Only use this slide if someone asks how the bigger array did.
33: Backup. A Monte Carlo check of p to the n. Each simulated array fills sixteen sites with independent coin flips at seventy or ninety-seven percent, repeated a hundred thousand times. The perfect-array fraction comes out at zero point three percent and sixty-one point three percent, matching the formula. The standard error at a hundred thousand trials is under zero point two percent, so it's not luck. The model assumes sites fail independently. Clustered defects, like one dirty patch, would make big arrays fail more often than p to the n predicts. Use this slide if someone questions the statistics.
